extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of aesthetics, poets, artists, and art critics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and evaluative principles for painting, sculpture, poetry, drama, and tragedy as discussed in a philosophical aesthetics text; aimed at guiding judgment of artistic quality and methods of representation. Covers technical, formal, and conceptual standards with examples and anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and originality in depicting human countenance
rubrics_metrics.description: If the features of a face 'lie within very narrow limits' and show essential unity and great originality, they likely originate from nature's inner being; an artist imagining such a face will produce at best a half-true or impossible composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: imagined faces are suspect; therefore in historical paintings only real portraits should figure, selected with the greatest care and 'in some degree idealised.' Anti-pattern: inventing physiognomies that may be contradictory or impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate aesthetic qualities in painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides conveying Ideas, painting possesses an independent beauty produced by harmony of colours, pleasing grouping, distribution of light and shade, and the tone of the whole picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These subordinate qualities further the condition of 'pure knowing' and are analogous to diction, metre, and rhyme in poetry: not essential but immediate. Evaluate paintings for these harmonies as contributing to, not replacing, the work's conceptual aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadmissibility (or risk) of allegory in painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory in painting can fail when viewers lack the requisite mythic or doctrinal knowledge; allegorical symbols ('kyriological hieroglyphic') may be unintelligible or misleading without shared background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Caravaggio's Christ treading the serpent; Giordano's ceiling allegory; these may be obscure to viewers unfamiliar with the underlying myths. Anti-pattern: using complex symbolic schemes that assume specialized knowledge and thereby alienate ordinary viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of visual arts representing sound or action (e.g., shrieking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plastic and pictorial arts are essentially dumb and cannot directly represent sounds like shrieking; literal depiction (open mouths) often produces a faulty or ludicrous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should depict circumstantial cues that make the absence or suppression of the sound plausible (Laocoön example: showing snake bite in the side so shrieking is impossible). Anti-pattern: painting multiple wide-open shrieking mouths, which appears absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as art that activates the reader's imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is 'the art of bringing the imagination into play by means of words' so that images are completed uniquely in each reader's mind, fitting their individuality, knowledge, and humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantage: poems can produce fuller, individualized pictures in readers; contrast with plastic arts which present one fixed form for all. Evaluate poetry by its ability to suggest images that readers can richly develop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that the poet truly knows what he represents
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must have known the subject he represents; the profundity and clarity of his knowledge determine the poem's quality ('as the poet's knowledge has been profound or superficial so will his poem be').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet is 'excellent' insofar as he correctly represents his original; anti-pattern: producing impressive-sounding poetry that lacks genuine understanding of its subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative accessibility: poetry vs plastic/pictorial arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and music produce more immediate and universal effects; plastic/pictorial arts often require more culture and knowledge to be appreciated and may leave common people cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider accessibility when evaluating art: rarity and cult value can elevate pictures, but their appreciation often demands time and learning. Example: masterpieces discovered in servants' halls unrecognized for generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre and rhyme as constraint and enabler
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre and rhyme are 'a fetter, but also a veil'—they restrict expression yet permit the poet to say things he otherwise might not; metre (rhythm) is nobler (a priori sensibility) while rhyme is an affair of empirical hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess when metre/rhyme contribute meaningfully versus when they distort thought. Anti-pattern: letting metre/rhyme dominate and force violence upon thought for the sake of sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme often forces thought vs unforced rhyme as mark of the true poet
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, poets often seek the thought for the rhyme or the rhyme for the thought; the genuine poet's rhymes appear unforced, with thoughts coming already in rhyme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicator of quality: rhymes that feel natural and effortless. Anti-patterns: lines where the rhyme is evidently sought (boutsrimés), or the thought is contorted to fit a rhyme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary nature and limits of rhyme; excess is pleonasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhyme is essentially binary—the effect is limited to a single recurrence of the same sound; further repetitions do not strengthen but may be an aesthetic pleonasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex rhyme schemes (octave rhyme, terza rima, sonnet) can impose needless difficulty and mental torture; evaluate whether form enriches or stunts the thought. Example: Shakespeare's sonnets avoid repetitive rhyme by varying rhymes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound-focused poetry without meaning ('doggerel')
rubrics_metrics.description: Verses that flatter the ear and neglect sense can exist; the sound of verse can satisfy even if the meaning is obscure or sacrificed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of poetry that prioritizes musical effect over semantic content. Example: Chinese dramas with sung verses that flatter the ear but have obscure meaning; choruses of Greek tragedy sometimes hard to make out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of poetic-only vocabulary as a disadvantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Languages that have many words usable only in poetry (or prohibit certain prose words) create a conventional poetic language of 'painted sensations' that fails to speak to the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether vocabulary resonates genuinely or remains a painted, conventional register that excludes feeling. Anti-pattern: overuse of poetic diction that feels foreign and inauthentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classic versus romantic poetry distinguished by motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Classic poetry knows motives that are purely human, actual, and natural; romantic poetry treats artificial, conventional, and imaginary motives (Christian mythus, chivalrous honour, hyperphysical amorousness), which can distort human relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess poems for whether their motives are grounded in human nature or in contrived/imaginary conventions; anti-pattern: romantic excesses producing ludicrous distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of concreteness when transferring scenes to antiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic or narrative poems that set scenes in ancient Greece or Rome often lose concreteness because modern knowledge of antiquity is fragmentary and not perceptual, forcing poets into abstraction and generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except skilled exceptions (Shakespeare), evaluate whether historicizing weakens individualisation and concreteness. Anti-pattern: relying on antiquity as a mere exotic backdrop leading to emptiness and tediousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyrical poetry may intentionally neglect logical connection for mood unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent gaps and lack of proper connection in odes and songs often reflect an intentional neglect of logical connection so that the unity of fundamental sensation or mood can prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing lyrics, distinguish between true incoherence and deliberate fragmentation serving a unified mood (example: Petrarch's Canzone). Evaluate based on whether the mood thread coheres the parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic aim: show nature and existence of man
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of drama is to exhibit, through significant characters in significant situations, 'what is the nature and existence of man'—either focusing on character (nature) or fate/action (existence); though separable in concept, they are inseparable in representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess dramas by how well character and action interrelate to reveal human nature; identify whether a work unfairly privileges one pole to the detriment of the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred dramactic structure: peace → motive chain → passionate climax
rubrics_metrics.description: A most complete dramatic form introduces characters in a state of peace (showing general colour), then introduces a motive which produces action, leading to stronger motives and actions until passionate excitement replaces original peace and significant actions reveal character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate plot construction by the quality of motive escalation and whether actions organically reveal character. Anti-pattern: sudden, unmotivated shifts without plausible motive chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of character-voice: transformative impersonation vs authorial intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Great poets 'transform themselves into each of the persons' and speak from each with truth and naturalness (ventriloquism). Poets of the second rank project themselves into principal persons, leaving other characters lifeless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure dramatic/poetic characterization by the distinctiveness and autonomy of each voice. Anti-pattern: all characters sounding like the author (Byron example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy evokes the sublime and leads to resignation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure in tragedy belongs to the sublime: by presenting the terrible, the tragic moves us to turn away from the will and its attachments, revealing that life is 'a bad dream' and provoking a resignation or surrender of the will to live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tragic works by their capacity to elevate the spectator beyond personal will and to reveal the world's insufficiency as ground for attachment. Distinguish forms: ancient tragedy often shows submission to fate but not surrender of will to live, whereas other religious contexts may present consolation beyond life.
